I am 46 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County my whole life. I finished middle school, which is enough to read seed packages and fertilizer labels. My family has about 8 mu of flat, irrigated land. Around here, the safest and most common system is the wheat–maize double crop. Everyone does it because the soil is good, we have wells for irrigation, and there are always buyers for both grains.

I will plant winter wheat this autumn on all 8 mu. Before sowing in mid-October, I will rotary till the field. I will buy an improved wheat seed variety. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea in spring. In total, I plan about 25 kg of nitrogen, 12 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu. The wheat will need four irrigations: one before winter to help it survive the cold, one at green-up in March, one at jointing, and one at heading. I will spray pesticides four times to control aphids, weeds, and fungal diseases. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat.

Right after harvesting the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize without any tillage—just direct seeding into the wheat stubble. I will use a hybrid maize seed. I will apply compound fertilizer at planting, giving roughly 15 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu. Maize needs less water than wheat here, so two irrigations are enough: one at the jointing stage and one during grain filling. I will spray pesticides three times for insects and weeds. I expect about 550 kg per mu from the maize.

I thought about cotton, but maize is more reliable and easier to manage with my limited labor. This plan keeps my land busy all year and gives me steady income.
